items.title: 9/11 Survivor’s Chilling Warning About ‘Evil’ 25 Years Later
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A former Secret Service agent who survived the Sept. 11 terror attacks is warning that he believes some Americans might not be gleaning important lessons from the deadly assault.

Darin Kinder said he “had a front row seat to evil” that fateful day, but that he also “saw the best of America” amid the terror.

“I was outside when the second impact happened 80-90 yards from the base of that tower,” he said. “And then scurried up into World Trade Tower OneIwith some other coworkers, helping people evacuate.”

Then, he was at the base of Tower Two when it buckled and collapsed. It was in that moment that Kinder faced a harrowing situation, as he was in a battle for his life.

“That began my mad dash for life,” he said. “That’s when I thought it was gone for sure. I thought it was game over.”

Kinder tried to outrun the tower’s collapse, struggling to breathe through the thick smoke. He was able to survive and flee the chaos and has spent the past 25 years sharing his story. His memoir, “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11,” has been one of the tools he has used to offer up his journey toward hope and healing.

Among the other topics he covered is courage, something he described as “a choice.” And as Kinder reflects on the hope he experienced amid so much pain, he also has a warning for Americans 25 years after radical Islam inflicted such pain on the nation: that some might have forgotten what unfolded.

“I think a September 10th mindset is kind of encroaching in, and where we just want to keep our head buried in the sand and not address the real evil that’s there, the real presence of a threat that’s there,” Kinder said. “And we can’t have that.”

He said he’s been bothered and concerned by some of what he’s seen among young people who are asking questions to which they should know the answers. Tragically, he said many of these people simply haven’t been educated on these matters, with the facts of what unfolded at the hands of “19 radical Islamic terrorists” being shielded or ignored.

Kinder also said other historic elements surrounding the event that “killed nearly 3,000 Americans and that kicked off a generational war — the global War on Terror — that we have seen the negative ripple and ramifications of” have also been largely ignored. He encouraged people to adhere to the truth, and warned that some Christians are too focused on the wrong elements.

“It’s this devout devotion to the 11th Commandment — ‘Thou shall be nice,'” Kinder said. “And it’s just not there. I mean, we’re we’re commanded to speak the truth in love and truth without love is harsh. Love without truth is just trying to be a nice guy that gets along to go-a-long. We have to be able to to to relay the truth to the next generation.”

Kinder said it’s often a temptation for Christians to want to be comfortable, yet Scripture shows Jesus and his followers weren’t always in that position. In fact, they were “hunted…chased out of town” and even beaten and stoned.

“We want to embrace comfort and not have real conversations,” he said, noting that the history of Islam was one of imposition at its roots, juxtaposing it against Christianity, which he called a “religion of invitation.” Understanding these realities, he said, is key.

“I would just say bluntly that evil doesn’t stop when you ask nicely,” he said. “And when it reaches its radical form and it’s literally attacking you physically or it’s undercutting everything in your culture and everything in your society and slowly changing over time that needs to be pushed back.”

Kinder continued, “That is darkness, and we’re called to bring light into dark.”

He encouraged Christians to “get engaged” and to stop burying their heads in the sand. Read more of his story in “Bury Me in a Dirty Suit: Discovering Man’s Valiant Purpose in the Aftermath Of 9/11.”

items.title: ‘Natural Realm Responded’: Filmmakers Detail Spiritual Manifestation on Set of New Movie
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

In Romans, the Apostle Paul wrote about the earth pointing to God’s “eternal power and divine nature.” The Koomans, two filmmaking brothers, certainly sensed that while making their newest movie, “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

It unfolded when Mena Massoud, portraying Daniel, and Elijah Alexander, playing King Nebuchadnezzar, filmed a scene on-location in India from Daniel 2, when the king — furious over astrologers who couldn’t interpret his dream — ordered Daniel’s execution. Facing his would-be killers, Daniel visited Nebuchadnezzar, asking for more time to petition God for an answer to the king’s dream “so they would not be executed along with the other wise men of Babylon” (Daniel 2:18, NLT).

When Massoud began reciting his lines, telling Nebuchadnezzar the meaning of his dream, Daniel and Matthew Kooman told CBN’s “Faith in Culture” the atmosphere on set shifted powerfully.

The scene centered on the latter part of Daniel 2, when Daniel foreshadowed the coming of Christ and what many biblical scholars believe to be a reference to Jesus’ triumphant return in the end times:

During the reigns of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or conquered. It will crush all these kingdoms into nothingness, and it will stand forever. That is the meaning of the rock cut from the mountain, though not by human hands, and crushed to pieces the statue of iron, bronze, clay, silver, and gold. The great God was showing the king what will happen in the future. The dream is true and its meaning is certain” (Daniel 2:44-45, NLT).

“[Massoud is] speaking these words from Scripture, and a wind blows across the set,” Daniel Kooman recalled. “Behind the camera, tents were hitting walls and blowing off set. A rainstorm, a crack of thunder — things that we hadn’t experienced in the natural realm on any day leading up to that for 25 days of prep and shooting. None of these sort of occurrences were happening until those words of Scripture about the everlasting kingdom that is coming [were spoken].”

“All of a sudden,” he said, “the natural realm responded to those words of prophetic Scripture.”

With an impressive $1.2 million raised in crowdfunding, the Koomans said they are confident audiences are eager for epic-style theatrical films like “Daniel and the Fiery Furnace.”

More importantly, Matthew Kooman told CBN News he is confident the project has divine backing.

“God was clearly behind it from the beginning,” he said. “And we were blown away by just the success of raising funds through people who wanted to be a part of telling the biblical story. That’s what the real synergy was.”

Trusting in the Lord — and standing by the courage of one’s convictions — is critical to success in Hollywood, the brothers said, particularly for filmmakers making content retelling biblical stories.

Calling the project “incredibly challenging,” Daniel Kooman said the one thing that kept him and his brother grounded was constant meditation on the source material, the Old Testament book of Daniel, and a genuine belief in the inerrancy of the totality of Scripture.

The movie pulls cross references from all throughout the Bible. In addition to Daniel, the film blends in scriptural accounts from the the books of Psalms, Isaiah, Habakkuk, and Jeremiah.

“We found practically … we couldn’t take one step on any given day without a leading or a direction from the Lord,” said Daniel Kooman. “That can sound abstract, but, for us, it was like, ‘OK, what are we gonna do today and how is it going to have an impact?’ It’s only gonna be if it honors the Word.”

Pointing to Isaiah 55:11, which says Scripture “always produces fruit” (NLT), Daniel Kooman said he noticed a one-to-one correlation that, when they dedicated themselves to accurately retelling the story of Daniel as it’s depicted in the Bible, “there was an incredible blessing.”

“People on set — actors and people involved in the production — experienced that,” he said. “It was a daily occurrence of God’s help through the production.”

items.title: Chandler Moore and Elevation Worship Just Cracked the Billboard Hot 100 — a First for Both
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: The Billboard Hot 100 has never exactly been worship music’s natural habitat. This week, Elevation Worship and Chandler Moore finally got in. “God I’m Just Grateful,” Elevation Worship’s collaboration with Moore, debuts at No. 91 on the chart dated Sept. 19. It’s the first Hot 100 appearance for eit
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The Billboard Hot 100 has never exactly been worship music’s natural habitat. This week, Elevation Worship and Chandler Moore finally got in.

“God I’m Just Grateful,” Elevation Worship’s collaboration with Moore, debuts at No. 91 on the chart dated Sept. 19. It’s the first Hot 100 appearance for either of them.

For Elevation, the omission was getting a little strange. Billboard named the group its Top Christian Artist of 2024, and “Praise” spent more than 25 weeks at No. 1 on Hot Christian Songs. It still never reached the Hot 100, eventually peaking at No. 5 on the Bubbling Under chart.

“God I’m Just Grateful” managed to make the jump. The song is currently No. 1 on Hot Christian Songs, where it has spent four straight weeks, and now it’s crossed onto Billboard’s all-genre ranking of the biggest songs in the country.

Here’s the song:

Historically, that crossover has been rare. When Billboard looked at the trend in May 2025, it found only 11 Christian songs since 2013 that had reached the Hot 100 after excluding holiday records and rap crossovers. Hillsong UNITED’s “Oceans” was the standout worship-band example. Brandon Lake and Forrest Frank both broke through in 2025 as Christian music started showing up on the chart more often.

Elevation Worship can now add its name to that history.

The song itself isn’t exactly coy about its subject: It’s called “God I’m Just Grateful,” and gratitude is pretty much the entire assignment. For Moore, it also arrives during a particularly personal stretch.

He left Maverick City Music last October after years as one of the collective’s defining voices. Then, earlier this month, he posted a clip of a new song about checking himself into rehab in November 2023, where he spent 40 days in treatment.

Now he has another career first.

items.title: Love God—Not His Benefits
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends for this Twenty-fifth Sunday in Ordinary Time, we hear a story from Jesus that tends to bother everybody: the parable of the laborers in the vineyard.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends for this Twenty-fifth Sunday in Ordinary Time, we hear a story from Jesus that tends to bother everybody: the parable of the laborers in the vineyard. We’re meant to hear our own voices in the complaint of these workers. Dealing with God, we often think things are unfair. Why does he do what he does? I’d like to get at this with a clarification that comes out of the heart of the spiritual tradition: You don’t fall in love with the benefits of God; you fall in love with God.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Isaiah 55:6-9

Seek the Lord while he may be found,
    call upon him while he is near;
let the wicked forsake their way,
    and the unrighteous their thoughts;
let them return to the Lord, that he may have mercy on them,
    and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
For my thoughts are not your thoughts,
    nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord.
For as the heavens are higher than the earth,
    so are my ways higher than your ways
    and my thoughts than your thoughts.

Psalm
Psalm 145:2-3, 8-9, 17-18

Every day I will bless you,
    and praise your name forever and ever.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised;
    his greatness is unsearchable.
The Lord is gracious and merciful,
    slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
The Lord is good to all,
    and his compassion is over all that he has made.
The Lord is just in all his ways,
    and kind in all his doings.
The Lord is near to all who call on him,
    to all who call on him in truth.

Second Reading
Philippians 1:20c-24, 27a

It is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be put to shame in any way, but that by my speaking with all boldness, Christ will be exalted now as always in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me, living is Christ and dying is gain. If I am to live in the flesh, that means fruitful labor for me; and I do not know which I prefer. I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for you.

Only, live your life in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ, so that, whether I come and see you or am absent and hear about you, I will know that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving side by side with one mind for the faith of the gospel,

Gospel Reading
Matthew 20:1-16a

“For the kingdom of heaven is like a landowner who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for the usual daily wage, he sent them into his vineyard. When he went out about nine o’clock, he saw others standing idle in the marketplace; and he said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard, and I will pay you whatever is right.’ So they went. When he went out again about noon and about three o’clock, he did the same. And about five o’clock he went out and found others standing around; and he said to them, ‘Why are you standing here idle all day?’ They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You also go into the vineyard.’ When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his manager, ‘Call the laborers and give them their pay, beginning with the last and then going to the first.’ When those hired about five o’clock came, each of them received the usual daily wage. Now when the first came, they thought they would receive more; but each of them also received the usual daily wage. And when they received it, they grumbled against the landowner, saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong; did you not agree with me for the usual daily wage? Take what belongs to you and go; I choose to give to this last the same as I give to you. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or are you envious because I am generous?’ So the last will be first, and the first will be last.”

items.title: The Broadcast Bishop: Fulton J. Sheen
items.author: Isabelle Larivee
items.summary:
Isabelle Larivee

Fulton Sheen was not afraid to be a Catholic, whether on a radio station or on television for millions, and the world of Catholic media owes it to him.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Isabelle Larivee

On September 24, a man already beloved by multitudes in the Catholic Church will finally receive the title of “Blessed.” Though not yet canonized, he is already a household name throughout the United States. He was the first television evangelist in history, with an influence so pivotal that the FBI kept a file on him for much of his life and America magazine called him “the greatest evangelizer in the history of the Catholic Church in the United States.” Perhaps America’s favorite priest, he is Bishop Fulton J. Sheen. 

On May 8, 1895, the first of four sons was born to Newton Morris Sheen and Delia Fulton in the second-floor apartment above Mr. Sheen’s hardware store in El Paso, Illinois. He was christened Peter John Sheen in the diocese of Peoria. Unfortunately, he was sickly as an infant and was usually taken care of by Delia’s side of the family, and so, when enrolled in school, he was enrolled as a Fulton. He eventually went by Fulton Sheen. 

As a boy, Fulton never desired any path other than the priesthood. When he was eight years old, he was altar serving for Mass with Bishop John Lancaster Spalding—the historic first bishop of Peoria and co-founder of the Catholic University of America (CUA)—as the celebrant. A cruet was dropped and smashed into pieces, and Bishop Spalding had a talk with the young future bishop after Mass. Somewhat out of the blue, Spalding predicted to the small, shaking altar boy that he would one day study in Louvain, Belgium. And then he said, “Someday, you will be just as I am.” 

Fulton attended high school at the bishop’s own Spalding Institute. Now a tall, slender figure, his intense blue eyes were so deeply set they looked black. He did well in the academic world and went on to St. Viator College followed by the Saint Paul Seminary in Minnesota. He was ordained on September 20, 1919, at the age of twenty-four but continued his studies at CUA. In 1921, Fr. Fulton Sheen did indeed go to Louvain, Belgium, to further his studies and then to Paris and Rome from 1923 to 1925. 

In 1926, when he was thirty-one, he taught theology at St. Edmund’s College in England. Former teachers of his recommended him for prestigious positions, but his bishop called him back to a small parish in Illinois. He was only there for eight months, however, before being assigned to teach at CUA. Fr. Sheen asked the bishop why he didn’t just send him immediately to CUA instead of waiting eight months. The bishop replied, “I was afraid you might become proud. I wanted to find out if you were obedient and would do what you were told.” Sheen would teach at the university for twenty-three years, and countless numbers of students and visitors would overflow in room 112 in McMahon Hall to hear a lecture by the revered professor. 

His reputation for speaking meandered off the campus, and in 1926, Fr. Fulton was asked to record a series of Sunday evening sermons for a New York radio station. In 1930, he was asked to fill in for an absence on the radio program, The Catholic Hour. What was supposed to be a two-week stint turned into a regular occurrence as the listeners couldn’t get enough of Fr. Sheen’s talks. He ended up speaking on the show for twenty more years. 

In addition to his classes and regular radio appearances, Fulton Sheen began teaching classes to converts, taking the train from Washington, DC, to New York almost every weekend. He also started preaching on street corners in the South, accompanied by a sign that read, “Questions cheerfully answered.” His work attracted more than a few, and in 1934, Pope Pius XI granted him the honored title “Monsignor” when he was only thirty-nine. 

In 1937, he wrote to the university’s rector, Msgr. Corrigan, and said,

During the past year letters demanding personal attention have run between 75 and 100 a day. . . . This coupled with classes never given with less than six hours preparation for each lecture has left me physically exhausted. However the good to be done is such that one dare not shrink from its opportunities for apostolate.

Msgr. Sheen did not slow down but spoke all over the United States and was a columnist for the secular press. On Easter Sunday 1940, he preached in history’s first televised Catholic religious service on what would later be New York’s WNBC. Ten years later, the beloved professor at last left the university and became the national director of the Society for the Propagation of the Faith.

On June 11, 1951, at the age of fifty-six, the monsignor was consecrated a bishop. That fall, Bishop Sheen launched his beloved television series Life is Worth Living. With an estimated thirty million viewers, it was the most widely-viewed religious TV series in the history of television. He was awarded an Emmy for Most Outstanding Television Personality and appeared on the cover of Time magazine. 

When filming, Sheen never used notes or prompters, but he did not credit his speaking as extemporaneous; each thirty minutes of showtime came from thirty hours of preparation. Ted Bergman from the DuMont Television Network said, “Bishop Fulton Sheen didn’t wear a watch. But he came out at 22:30 every single time out. How he did it, I never knew. I finally went to him and said, ‘Your Excellency, how can you do this? Do you have a clock in your head?’ He said, ‘When you’ve been teaching as long as I have, you know exactly how long to talk.’” 

In 1966, when his radio and television presence had progressed for some forty years, he was assigned to be the bishop of Rochester at seventy-one years old. Sheen had always been very absorbed in the plight of the poor, and that certainly didn’t change now, but, for unclear reasons, the diocese of Rochester didn’t want to pursue that mission with him. Among other disagreements, Bishop Sheen had requested that every parish set aside five percent for the needy, but not every parish followed his lead right away. There were objections, and they wanted to talk about it. 

During Sheen’s term as Bishop of Rochester, everyone felt they needed to be listened to; everyone had an opinion, and it needed to be heard. Sheen, on the other hand, was from a generation of priests who simply did what their bishop asked of them. They were from the generation of dialogue—he was not. He resigned in 1969, stating, “I am not retiring, only retreading.” 

He began spending his time giving retreats for priests in America, Canada, England, and Ireland. He was very concerned about the loss of priestly identity he was witnessing. The alter Christus, sacrificial nature of a priest was being forgotten, drowned out by social work and apostolates. Distracted from Christ, there was a growing crisis of priestly identity, and vocations were plummeting. His chief recommendation was for priests to spend an hour in front of the Blessed Sacrament every day; for the laity, he prescribed at least thirty minutes. 
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

After a long battle with heart disease, Bishop Sheen went in for open-heart surgery in July 1977. From that point on, he began slowing down, and his public appearances lessened. Two years later, on October 2, 1979, a crowd of Catholics filled St. Patrick’s Cathedral in New York. His Holiness, John Paul II, would be giving an audience there soon, but hadn’t arrived yet. An eighty-four-year-old bishop entered the church, and, recognized by everyone there as their beloved Bishop Sheen, applause erupted from the entire congregation. This would be his last public appearance. When the pope arrived, he called Fulton J. Sheen forward. He hugged him, and as the two future saints embraced, the pope said, “You have written and spoken well of the Lord Jesus. You are a loyal son of the Church!” 

On October 11, 1979, Pope John Paul II wrote to Fulton Sheen, congratulating him on his six decades as a priest: “God called you to proclaim in an extraordinary way his dynamic word . . . in these six decades of your priestly service, God has touched the lives of millions of the men and women of our time.” Sheen wrote back, “I bow in humble gratitude for the Pontifical approval of my ministry of the Word.” 

On December 9 of that year, the beloved bishop died on the floor of his private chapel in front of the Blessed Sacrament, likely praying his holy hour as he had always done. 

In all, he wrote sixty-six books and was responsible for countless conversions, including several well‑known celebrities. He had raised millions for the Catholic missions, and no one could deny the influence he had. In Vatican II, he had worked very closely with the future Benedict XVI, who later recalled in a 2012 interview, “Fulton Sheen . . . would fascinate us in the evenings with his talks.” 

He had all the prominence, all the intellect, and all the diplomacy to be a cardinal, but he was never elevated to that rank. This fact perplexed many people, and in a 60 Minutes interview with Mike Wallace, Sheen was asked why he thought this was the case. The bishop hinted that he could have risen, had he wanted to pull strings. Wallace asked him, “Are you an ambitious man?” Sheen thought and answered, “I suppose there certainly must be ambition in me, because ambition is really, in a certain sense, drive for perfection. But I have never deliberately sought any kind of honor. It is possible for a man in the church to go up and up, and I could have gone higher and higher and higher. But I refused to pay the price.” Evidently, there were church politics that Sheen didn’t want to be a part of, but he never spoke about it. 

His lack of cardinal status did not diminish the scope and success of his mission nor the endurance of his legacy. The education archivist for CUA said, “Catholics had pretty much been excluded at the national level . . . he instilled in them a sense of confidence that enabled their inclusion into American society.” 

Fr. Charles Connor, an accomplished church historian, was asked what we can learn from Sheen’s legacy, to which he replied, “The lesson that can be learned is: Be Catholic. Be authentically Catholic, nothing but Catholic, and don’t water down . . . be what you are, and nothing less than what you are.”

Bishop Fulton Sheen was not afraid to be a Catholic, whether that be on a local radio station or on television for an audience of thirty million, and the modern world of Catholic media in America owes it all to him. There are now more Catholic radio programs than ever before, even more televised and online sermons, and the presence of the Church in the world of media now seems like a given—but Bishop Sheen was the first to do it all. 

He gave a resounding voice to Catholics—and who could forget that voice? Who could forget his words, so grave yet, at times, so comical? Who could forget his deep-set stare, so austere yet so bright? Who could forget his theatrical way of speaking and the flourish of his writing on his ever-present chalkboard? It seems fitting to close with the unforgettable words that the beloved Sheen used to end every episode: “Good-bye now, and God love you!”
